sections.history: Tiruvedagam is a village on the Vaigai in Madurai district, some 18 to 20 km from Madurai city and a few kilometres from Sholavandan. The temple is praised in a decad of Tirugnana Sambandar in the third Tirumurai, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam. The original complex is believed to have been raised by the Pandyas, and the present masonry is attributed to the Madurai Nayaks of the sixteenth century; inscriptions here are linked to the later Pandya and Vijayanagara periods. The shrine is bound to a turning point in Shaiva history, the visit of Sambandar to the Pandya court at Madurai in the reign of King Arikesari Nedumaran, when the king, drawn toward Jainism, was won back to Shaiva faith. Tellings of that episode differ in their details, but tradition places this riverside shrine at the point where the contest's most famous sign came to rest.
sections.architecture: The temple stands on the northern bank of the Vaigai, across roughly five acres, with two gopurams, each leading to its own sanctum. The sanctum of Edaganathar holds the Shiva linga, while the goddess Elavarkuzhali is honoured in her own shrine to the right of the main sanctum. Spacious corridors run around the shrines. A shrine of Vinayaka, remembered as the Vinayaka who won the debate (Vaaduvenra Vinayagar), belongs to the legend of the palm leaf. The river beside the temple lends the place the atmosphere of a sacred bathing ghat.
sections.legends: The defining story of Tiruvedagam belongs to the contest between Tirugnana Sambandar and the Jains at Madurai. In the trial by water, each side set a palm leaf (olai) bearing its verses upon the flood of the Vaigai. The Jains' leaf was swept away by the current; Sambandar's, inscribed with his hymn, turned and travelled upstream against the flow. Tradition says the Pandya minister Kulachiraiyar followed it until it halted at this spot, and that Vinayaka, in the form of a fish, stopped the leaf here. The place came to be called Tiruvedagam, the sacred place of the leaf, where the hymn had reached. Other tellings add a trial by fire in which Sambandar's leaf did not burn; the details vary, but faith in the power of the hymn runs through them all.
sections.festivals: The most prominent festival is the Muthu Pandal festival, held around Magam in February or March, and the temple keeps four main festivals through the year. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple, and the Tamil-month festivals are kept with devotion. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Come to Tiruvedagam as a pilgrim of the river. Walk first down to the bank of the Vaigai, where the leaf is said to have come ashore, and let the story settle before you enter. Pass beneath the gopuram to the sanctum of Edaganathar, then turn to Elavarkuzhali in her own shrine to the right of the main sanctum, and pause before the Vinayaka of the legend. The temple lies a little apart from the bustle of the city, and its quiet suits a longer stay.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning (roughly 6:30 to 12:00) and again from late afternoon into the evening (roughly 5:00 to 8:00), with a midday break; listings vary, so confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tiruvedagam lies on the Vaigai about 18 to 20 km from Madurai and 3 to 5 km from Sholavandan, the nearest railway station. City buses from Madurai's Periyar and Anna bus stands serve the village, with routes such as 29A, 54A, 63, 65 and 68 from Periyar; confirm routes locally. The nearest airport is at Madurai.
